paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until relatively recently, it was thought that the depictions of animals found on the walls of the renowned Altamira, Lascaux, and Chauvet caves in southern Europe, which date from 16,000 to 40,000 years ago, were created by Homo sapiens – humans like ‘us’. It was assumed the drawings were the expression of modern man, a superior species which crossed to Europe from Africa around 45,000 years ago, driving out the crude, artless Neanderthal species which had been living on the continent for hundreds of thousands of years before that.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: It turns out that the story is a good deal more complicated, and more interesting. It begins, as these things often do, in Africa. One day in 2000, archaeologist Christopher Henshilwood and his team were excavating Blombos Cave in South Africa when they dug out a small block of engraved reddish-yellow rock known as ochre. Ochre is common in this part of Africa and has been used for millennia for everything from preserving food to painting bodies. This piece, though, was different: roughly 75,000 years in the past, someone had carefully etched on it a pattern of overlapping, parallel, triangular markings. Whatever their elusive purpose, they were 35,000 years older than any other undisputed evidence of symbolic behavior known at the time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Controversy dogged the Blombos discovery at first. Some scientists attacked the little rock as meaningless. In time, however, others regarded the discovery of the decorated rock as a breakthrough. Soon more examples of symbol and ornament were uncovered. Henshilwood’s team found shells of sea snails that were around 75,000 years old and perforated, indicating that they had been strung together to create jewellery. Very similar examples also appeared as far away as Morocco and Israel, some of them dating back to 100,000 years ago. The Blombos excavation also unearthed finely carved and decorated tools, an indication that as long as 100,000 years ago the cave’s inhabitants had methodically ground ochre and mixed it with other ingredients to make a paste. Stored in abalone shells – the earliest known containers – it could have been used to decorate a variety of items.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: What is particularly intriguing about these early African and Middle Eastern eruptions of symbolism is that they come and they go. In each case, the artefacts appear in the archaeological record for a few thousand years, and then disappear. The same applies to technological ideas and inventions. Bone harpoon points, found nowhere else before 45,000 years ago, have been uncovered in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in sediments nearly twice that old. In South Africa, two relatively complex stone and bone tool traditions emerge and then disappear. The Still Bay tradition appeared 75,000 years ago and lasted just 4,000 years, while the Howiesons Poort tradition, which dates from 65,000 years ago, lasted 6,000 years. Nowhere has a tradition been found to spread across locations and through time, gathering richness and diversity, until just before 40,000 years ago, when art began to appear more commonly across Africa, Eurasia, and Australasia.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It seems unlikely, therefore, that some genetic ‘switch’ flipped in our African ancestors to produce the capacity for a new, higher-order level of cognition that, once it evolved, produced a lasting change in human behaviour. So how do we explain these apparently sporadic bursts of creativity? One hypothesis is that the cause was not a new kind of person but a greater density of people, with spikes in population sparking contact between groups. This accelerated the spread of ideas from one mind to another, creating a kind of collective brain. Symbols would have helped cement this collective brain together. However, when populations again fell below critical mass, groups became isolated, leaving new ideas nowhere to go. What innovations had been established withered and died.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One thing that is clear is that soon after modern humans arrived in Europe around 45,000 years ago, the continent’s long-term residents began to die out. The Neanderthals had emerged in Eurasia some 200,000 years earlier. Very little evidence remains that they engaged in symbolic behaviour. But the traditional view of Neanderthals as brutish beings incapable of such behaviour has been slowly chipped away. For decades the debate over the Neanderthals’ ability to rise to the standards of their successors centred on a cave in France called Grotte du Renne, where artefacts normally associated with modern humans – tools, distinctive stone blades, and pierced and grooved animal teeth probably worn as pendants – were found alongside the remains of Neanderthals. The evidence suggested that the artefacts had been created by Neanderthals.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Some researchers reasoned that although the Neanderthals may have been responsible for making decorative objects, they were still a species capable only of emulating the elaborate craftsmanship of their new modern human neighbours, not inventing it on their own. However, the more we learn about Neanderthals, the more the ‘copycat’ explanation seems unlikely, but it is discernible. Some scholars argue that Neanderthal skeletons found in France and Iraq were intentionally buried. Markings recently found on bird-wing bones hint that Neanderthals used feathers for ornaments up to 50,000 years ago. And a single red disc painted on a wall in El Castillo Cave in Spain was recently dated to about 41,000 years ago, tantalisingly close to a time when only Neanderthals are known to have been in western Europe. Perhaps they, not us, were the first cave artists.
